case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under Atkins v. Virginia and later Supreme Court decisions, a habeas court may consider additional evidence of intellectual disability (including adaptive deficits) when a capital petitioner presents valid IQ scores in the 70–75 range, or whether such scores categorically bar Atkins relief.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment (as interpreted in Atkins v. Virginia) and the federal habeas review constraints of 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA) (with related references to § 2254(e)(2) on evidentiary hearings).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Commissioner (Alabama) argues that Smith either failed to properly preserve/present the federal claim by shifting his theory (thus barring federal review), and in any event that the state courts did not act contrary to or unreasonably apply clearly established Supreme Court law under AEDPA. On the merits, the State’s position (as framed by the Question Presented and amici materials) is that IQ scores in the 70–75 range should prevent a finding of intellectual disability (or at least preclude moving on to adaptive-deficits evidence in a way that would justify habeas relief), and that the Eleventh Circuit wrongly allowed consideration of additional evidence to reach an Atkins finding.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Smith argues that Atkins and its progeny require courts to consider the broader clinical picture—including adaptive functioning deficits—and do not impose a categorical IQ cutoff that bars relief when valid scores fall in the 70–75 range. He contends that the district court correctly weighed multiple IQ scores (including pre- and post-18 scores ranging roughly from 72 to 78) together with evidence of adaptive deficits, and that the Eleventh Circuit properly affirmed habeas relief under the controlling Supreme Court framework.
key_precedents: Harrington v. Richter, 562 U.S. 86 (2011) (cited in excerpt as 131 S. Ct. 770)
Kelley v. Sec’y for Dep’t of Corr., 377 F.3d 1317 (11th Cir. 2004)
Williams v. McNeil, 2010 WL 144986 (N.D. Fla. Jan. 7, 2010)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s § 2254(d)(1) timing point is the best argument on the other side, and I agree we cannot treat Hall or Moore as retroactively supplying “clearly established” law; Richter requires real deference in close cases. But I remain persuaded (as Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor emphasize) that Atkins itself clearly established a categorical Eighth Amendment protection keyed to the clinical concept of intellectual disability, and a state framework that makes an IQ score in the borderline low-70s effectively dispositive—thereby foreclosing consideration of the very adaptive-functioning evidence Atkins presupposes—can be an unreasonable application of that core holding even under fairminded-jurist review. Justice Alito’s Pinholster concern does not defeat that conclusion because the error I see is methodological on the state court’s own terms: a threshold gate that prevents reaching the constitutional question on the existing record, not federal reweighing under later standards. I would keep the opinion narrow: we do not constitutionalize SEM arithmetic or clinical minutiae; we hold only that a rigid cutoff in the borderline range that blocks meaningful adjudication of an Atkins claim is beyond the discretion Atkins left the States.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s argument that Atkins itself forbids any “structural gate” making a low-70s IQ score dispositive rests on importing a procedural requirement that Atkins did not articulate and, indeed, disclaimed by leaving “to the States” the means of enforcement. Justice Kavanaugh’s § 2254(d)(1) timing point reinforces that Hall and Moore cannot be used—whether labeled “confirmation” or not—to convert a debatable state implementation into an “unreasonable” application at the time, and Richter requires deference wherever fairminded jurists could read Atkins’s delegation to permit reliance on threshold IQ practices in close cases. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s foreclosure/risk-of-error concerns are policy arguments about best practices and clinical evolution, but AEDPA does not authorize federal habeas courts to correct arguable methodological mistakes absent clearly established Supreme Court law. Pinholster further cautions against the Eleventh Circuit’s effective reweighing of the record under later-refined standards rather than assessing the reasonableness of the state court’s adjudication as it stood.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “structural foreclosure” framing is the strongest respondent point, but it still cannot overcome AEDPA’s temporal constraint: Atkins expressly left implementation to the States, and at the time of the state decision it did not clearly establish that SEM adjustment or a non-dispositive IQ threshold was constitutionally required under § 2254(d)(1). Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan rely on Hall/Moore as “confirmation,” yet that effectively imports later doctrinal and clinical refinements into the Richter fairminded-jurist inquiry, turning habeas review into error correction. Justice Gorsuch’s point that the state’s methodology itself is the defect does not move me because Atkins did not clearly forbid a threshold approach in close cases, and Pinholster reinforces that federal courts may not reweigh a contested clinical record under later-articulated standards. Even if a rigid cutoff is unwise as a policy matter, it is not enough to say the state court’s application was beyond fairminded disagreement on the law as it stood then.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s § 2254(d)(1) timing point is the strongest counter: Hall and Moore cannot retroactively create “clearly established” law, and Richter requires deference where fairminded jurists can disagree. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts (and Justice Kagan) that the relevant constraint is already in Atkins: once the Eighth Amendment adopts the clinical concept of intellectual disability as a categorical bar, a State unreasonably applies Atkins when it uses an effectively dispositive IQ gate in the borderline range to foreclose consideration of adaptive-functioning evidence central to that concept. Justice Alito’s Pinholster concern does not answer the antecedent defect because the error is methodological—structural exclusion of probative evidence on the existing state record—rather than federal supplementation or reweighing. Under a pragmatic, impacts-focused approach, AEDPA deference cannot extend to a framework that predictably creates an intolerable risk of executing people the Constitution protects.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s AEDPA timing argument is the hardest: § 2254(d)(1) is temporal, Richter is unforgiving, and Hall/Moore cannot supply “clearly established” law after the fact. But I agree with the Chief Justice that we can resolve this on Atkins alone: once Atkins constitutionalized a categorical Eighth Amendment bar keyed to the clinical construct of intellectual disability, a state cannot implement that bar through a rule that makes an IQ number effectively dispositive in the borderline range and thereby structurally forecloses consideration of SEM and adaptive-functioning evidence central to the constitutional inquiry. That is not using Hall/Moore retroactively; it is identifying an unreasonable application where the state’s methodology substitutes a numeric gate for the constitutionally required inquiry, which goes beyond fairminded disagreement even under Richter. Justice Alito’s Pinholster point does not change this because the defect is apparent in the state court’s own threshold approach—an evidentiary foreclosure—rather than a federal court’s supplementation or reweighing of the record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s § 2254(d)(1) timing objection is the strongest point for the Petitioner, but it does not carry the day because the “clearly established” rule we apply can come from Atkins itself: a categorical Eighth Amendment exemption keyed to the clinical concept of intellectual disability cannot be implemented through a dispositive IQ gate in the borderline range that forecloses the constitutionally required inquiry into intellectual and adaptive functioning. Justice Thomas is right that Atkins left “to the States” the task of enforcement, yet that delegation cannot be read to authorize a framework that structurally prevents adjudication of the very constitutional claim Atkins recognized—an unreasonable application even under Richter’s fairminded-jurist standard. Justice Alito’s Pinholster concern does not defeat relief where the legal error is the state court’s own stated methodology of evidentiary foreclosure; we can identify the unreasonable application on the existing record without importing Hall or Moore as new controlling law. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow formulation best preserves AEDPA’s temporal limits while still enforcing Atkins’s core protection against a rigid cutoff that creates an intolerable risk of executing a person the Constitution protects.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s “structural foreclosure” argument seriously, and I agree Hall and Moore can be read as confirming that a rigid IQ gate is problematic as a matter of Eighth Amendment merits. But under § 2254(d)(1), Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to stress Richter’s temporal, fairminded-jurist standard: Atkins expressly left implementation to the States, and at the time of the state decision it was not clearly established that SEM must be considered or that an IQ score in the low-70s could not be used as a threshold screen. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s effort to locate a no-cutoff rule “within Atkins itself” reads Atkins at a level of specificity that, in my view, collapses the distinction between later doctrinal refinement and clearly established law, effectively turning AEDPA into appellate error correction. On this record, the Eleventh Circuit’s grant of relief therefore exceeds AEDPA’s limited role even if I might agree with respondents on de novo Eighth Amendment policy.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “structural foreclosure” argument is the strongest for Respondent, but I do not think Atkins—given its express instruction that the States would develop “appropriate ways” to enforce the restriction—clearly established, for § 2254(d)(1) purposes, that borderline IQ scores require SEM accounting and mandatory consideration of adaptive functioning at the threshold. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, Hall and Moore cannot retroactively supply the needed specificity, and under Richter we may not label a debatable implementation choice “unreasonable” simply because later cases (or current clinical best practices) would reject it. Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan argue that Atkins itself “constitutionalized a clinical concept” and thus forbids a dispositive IQ gate, but that characterization effectively imports the later Hall/Moore methodology into Atkins rather than identifying a preexisting, clearly established rule with sufficient determinacy to overcome AEDPA deference. On this record—where the state court appears to have considered multiple IQ scores and some adaptive evidence rather than applying a facially absolute cutoff—the Eleventh Circuit’s relief risks becoming impermissible error correction under Pinholster/Richter.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Barrett’s § 2254(d)(1) timing objection is the strongest point for the Petitioner: Hall and Moore cannot do the “clearly established” work retroactively, and Richter requires deference where fairminded jurists could disagree. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that the constitutional defect can be identified within Atkins itself: once the Eighth Amendment adopts a categorical bar keyed to a clinical construct, a state may not implement that bar through a framework that makes a borderline IQ number effectively dispositive and thereby forecloses consideration of SEM and adaptive-functioning evidence central to the Atkins inquiry. That is not importing Hall/Moore as new law; it is recognizing that a gatekeeping rule that structurally prevents adjudication of the protected category is an unreasonable application of Atkins even under AEDPA. Justice Alito’s Pinholster concern about record expansion does not answer the threshold problem here, because the unreasonableness lies in the state court’s methodology that excludes constitutionally relevant evidence on the record it already had.

John Roberts.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia forbids execution of the intellectually disabled but leaves States discretion to implement diagnostic criteria, and Hall v. Florida later made clear that the Eighth Amendment prohibits a rigid IQ cutoff that bars consideration of the standard error of measurement and related evidence, including adaptive functioning. Given that framework, valid IQ scores in the 70–75 range cannot categorically preclude an Atkins claim; the inquiry must permit consideration of adaptive-deficits evidence consistent with clinical standards. Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), a state-court rule functioning as a categorical bar at 70 despite Hall’s instruction would be an unreasonable application of clearly established law, so habeas relief may stand on that narrow ground. This approach respects precedent and yields a limited holding: no categorical IQ-bar, without dictating a comprehensive state diagnostic regime.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under AEDPA, federal habeas relief is unavailable unless the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court holdings. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor; Lockyer v. Andrade. Atkins held only that the Eighth Amendment bars execution of the intellectually disabled and left to the States the task of developing standards; it did not clearly establish any rule requiring a habeas court to move beyond valid IQ scores in the 70–75 range to find disability, nor did it mandate particular treatment of adaptive-deficits evidence. Given Richter’s admonition that relief is barred so long as fairminded jurists could disagree, the Eleventh Circuit erred by effectively substituting its own weighing of new evidence for the state court’s reasonable application of Atkins within the deference demanded by § 2254(d).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal habeas court may not grant relief unless the state-court decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor; Harrington v. Richter. Atkins v. Virginia left substantial discretion to the States to develop mechanisms and standards for identifying intellectual disability, and it did not clearly establish that a State unconstitutionally applies Atkins by treating valid IQ scores in the 70–75 range as dispositive in a particular case. Given Pinholster’s limitation to the state-court record and AEDPA’s requirement of deference, the Eleventh Circuit’s approach risks converting disputed clinical judgments into de novo federal review rather than asking only whether the state court’s adjudication was unreasonable.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia forbids executing the intellectually disabled, and Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas make clear the Eighth Amendment does not tolerate rigid IQ cutoffs that prevent courts from considering the standard error of measurement and the full clinical picture, including adaptive-functioning deficits. Where a petitioner presents valid IQ scores in the low 70s and evidence of significant adaptive deficits, a habeas court may not treat the 70–75 range as a categorical bar; doing so would unreasonably apply clearly established Eighth Amendment principles as articulated in Hall and Moore. AEDPA, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), does not require federal courts to rubber-stamp state rules that structurally exclude relevant clinical evidence central to an Atkins determination. The practical consequence of the State’s position is a substantial risk of executing a person the Constitution protects, a risk Hall and Moore were designed to prevent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia bars executing the intellectually disabled but deliberately left States latitude to implement workable standards, and nothing in Atkins clearly established a categorical rule that valid IQ scores in the 70–75 range foreclose consideration of adaptive-functioning evidence. Later decisions like Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas reject rigid IQ cutoffs and require attention to the standard error of measurement and the broader clinical picture, reinforcing that intellectual-disability determinations cannot turn on a single number alone. Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), the question is whether the state court unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court law; a state rule treating 70–75 as an absolute bar is difficult to square with Atkins’s framework as clarified by Hall, and a habeas court may consider additional evidence to assess the claim. Any procedural “theory-shift” argument does not justify insulating an Eighth Amendment protection from review where the core Atkins claim—intellectual disability barring execution—was presented and adjudicated.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia left the States some implementation discretion but anchored the constitutional inquiry in the clinical concept of intellectual disability, and Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas make clear the Eighth Amendment forbids rigid IQ cutoffs that treat scores as precise and bar consideration of adaptive-functioning evidence when the score range implicates the disability threshold. Nothing in Atkins or its progeny establishes a categorical rule that valid IQ scores in the 70–75 range foreclose an Atkins claim; to the contrary, Hall requires accounting for the standard error of measurement and proceeding to the broader clinical picture rather than stopping at a number. Under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), a state court that treats a score in this range as an absolute bar unreasonably applies clearly established law as articulated in Hall and Moore, and a habeas court may consider additional evidence necessary to adjudicate the federal constitutional claim (subject to § 2254(e)(2)’s limits). Given the Eighth Amendment’s categorical protection recognized in Atkins, any remaining ambiguity about thresholds should not be resolved by an inflexible rule that risks executing the intellectually disabled.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under AEDPA, the question is not the best reading of Atkins but whether the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law at the time. Atkins (2002) held the Eighth Amendment bars executing the intellectually disabled but left to the States the task of developing workable procedures and did not clearly establish that IQ scores in the 70–75 range must be treated as satisfying the intellectual-functioning prong or that habeas courts must proceed to adaptive-deficits evidence notwithstanding a State’s threshold rule. Later decisions like Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas, which rejected rigid IQ cutoffs and required attention to the SEM and clinical standards, cannot be used to deem earlier state-court decisions unreasonable under § 2254(d)(1). Given Richter’s admonition that relief is unavailable unless no fairminded jurist could agree with the state court, the Eleventh Circuit’s grant of relief exceeded AEDPA’s narrow scope.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal habeas court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter, 562 U.S. 86 (2011). Atkins v. Virginia left substantial implementation discretion to the States, and Hall v. Florida (and later Moore v. Texas) prohibits rigid IQ cutoffs that foreclose consideration of the standard error of measurement and adaptive functioning, but those decisions do not clearly establish that valid IQ scores in the 70–75 range compel an Atkins finding or require a federal court to reweigh the clinical evidence on habeas. Given that the asserted entitlement here depends on how multiple IQ scores and adaptive-deficits evidence should be weighed, the state court’s application is at least within the range of reasonable disagreement, and § 2254(d)(1) therefore bars relief.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia bars execution of intellectually disabled persons, and Hall v. Florida makes clear the Eighth Amendment forbids rigid IQ cutoffs that treat scores near 70 as categorically dispositive; courts must account for the standard error of measurement and proceed to consider adaptive-functioning evidence when the score range overlaps the clinical threshold. Given that framework, valid IQ scores in the 70–75 range cannot, by themselves, bar consideration of additional evidence of adaptive deficits, and a contrary state-court approach would be an unreasonable application of clearly established law under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1). This approach also promotes procedural fairness by ensuring the Atkins inquiry reflects the “broader clinical picture,” rather than an arbitrary numerical line. Accordingly, habeas relief is not foreclosed merely because some valid scores fall above 70, and the federal court may evaluate the full record consistent with Hall and Atkins.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under Atkins v. Virginia and subsequent Supreme Court decisions, a habeas court may consider adaptive-functioning and other intellectual-disability evidence when a capital petitioner’s valid IQ scores fall in the 70–75 range (rather than at or below 70).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment (as interpreted in Atkins v. Virginia, and later intellectual-disability death-penalty cases), applied through federal habeas review limits in 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1) (AEDPA).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Commissioner (Alabama DOC) argues that federal courts should not treat IQ scores in the 70–75 range as sufficient to proceed to broader intellectual-disability proof in a way that overrides or second-guesses the state court’s determination under AEDPA; in addition, the briefing excerpts suggest an argument that Smith altered or failed to properly preserve the legal theory presented to the state courts, which would bar or limit federal habeas review, and that in any event the Eleventh Circuit affirmed habeas relief by applying Atkins and its progeny too expansively or without proper AEDPA deference.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Smith argues that Atkins and its progeny require courts to consider the full clinical picture—including adaptive deficits and other evidence—especially where valid IQ scores are within the measurement-error range around 70; therefore, the district court properly evaluated additional intellectual-disability evidence after finding qualifying IQ scores (74/75 pre-18; 72/74/78 post-18), and the Eleventh Circuit correctly affirmed habeas relief under Atkins.
key_precedents: Kelley v. Sec’y for Dep’t of Corr., 377 F.3d 1317 (11th Cir. 2004)
Neelley v. Nagle, 138 F.3d 917 (11th Cir. 1998) (abrogated in part as recognized by Parker v. Head)
Williams v. McNeil, 2010 WL 144986 (N.D. Fla. Jan. 7, 2010)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan most forcefully argue that the state court’s approach functioned as the kind of IQ-70 “gate” Hall forbids, and that AEDPA cannot shield an unconstitutional cutoff that forecloses adaptive-functioning consideration. But even accepting Hall’s anti-bright-line principle at a high level, Richter/Lockyer require us to ask whether the state court’s *disposition* was objectively unreasonable under clearly established holdings—not whether we would demand a fuller, more clinically rigorous inquiry on direct review—and fairminded jurists could disagree about whether this record reflects a conclusive 70-cutoff versus a broader evaluation of multiple scores and other evidence within Atkins’s implementation space. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Brumfield underscores that some threshold denials can be unreasonable, but it does not clearly establish an outcome-determinative rule that any SEM-overlapping score compels a full adaptive-functioning adjudication on habeas. A narrow AEDPA-based reversal best preserves institutional legitimacy while leaving the merits standards for initial Atkins/Hall litigation to direct review and state courts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Hall forbids an IQ-70 bright line that forecloses consideration of SEM and adaptive functioning, and they argue AEDPA cannot insulate a decision infected by that cutoff. But that framing assumes the state court applied Hall’s specific prohibition, rather than applying Atkins’s broader, state-discretionary framework to multiple scores and the overall record—precisely the kind of debatable application Richter and Lockyer say federal habeas courts may not second-guess absent an unmistakable, outcome-determinative holding. Even if Hall would control on direct review, § 2254(d)(1) ties “clearly established” law to the holdings governing the relevant state-court adjudication, and (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize) it does not clearly establish that every borderline score in the 70–75 range compels reopening adaptive-functioning proof regardless of how the state court assessed the evidence. Brumfield does not change that conclusion here: it turned on an unreasonable refusal to develop the record in the face of compelling indicia, not a mandate that federal courts override reasonable state judgments whenever SEM overlap exists.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan persuasively frame Hall as condemning any “70-as-dispositive” gate that prevents reaching adaptive functioning, and if the state court had plainly done that, the merits problem would be serious. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes under Richter and Lockyer, § 2254(d)(1) asks whether the state court’s adjudication was objectively unreasonable in light of clearly established holdings—not whether Hall’s anti-bright-line principle should be operationalized into a mandatory, stepwise clinical protocol whenever an SEM-adjusted range touches 70. On this record, fairminded jurists could characterize the state court as considering multiple scores and other evidence rather than applying a conclusive cutoff, which keeps the case within Atkins’s implementation space and outside habeas correction. Brumfield, as Justice Barrett notes, illustrates that some threshold denials can be unreasonable, but it does not clearly establish the outcome-determinative rule Respondent needs to overcome AEDPA deference here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito press the hardest point: under Richter/Lockyer, AEDPA bars relief if fairminded jurists could disagree, and Atkins left States implementation space. But Hall clearly established more than an aspirational “anti-bright-line principle”: it held that treating 70 as dispositive—by ignoring the SEM and thereby foreclosing any adaptive-functioning inquiry for borderline scores—creates an unconstitutional risk, and insulating that gatekeeping rule is an unreasonable application of Hall rather than mere evidentiary reweighing. Justice Gorsuch’s characterization that the state court “considered multiple scores” does not answer the core defect if the analysis still functionally ends the case at prong one once a score is pegged above 70 without SEM-adjustment, which is precisely what Hall forbids. Brumfield, as Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson note, supports requiring the State to proceed to the fuller inquiry when the threshold screen is infected by an impermissible cutoff, even on habeas, because the consequence is irrevocable and the constitutional prohibition is categorical.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’ strongest point is the Richter/Lockyer constraint: on habeas we cannot convert Hall into a detailed clinical protocol, and relief is barred if fairminded jurists could disagree about the state court’s application. But that deference still presupposes the state court did not apply the very categorical exclusion Hall held unconstitutional—treating 70 as dispositive by ignoring SEM such that the adaptive-functioning inquiry is foreclosed despite a score whose SEM-adjusted range reaches 70. Justice Gorsuch’s concern that the state court may have “considered multiple scores and other record evidence” matters only if the court actually engaged the SEM and permitted the fuller Atkins inquiry; where the step-one screen functions as a bright-line gate, the adjudication is an unreasonable application of clearly established law rather than mere evidentiary weighing. Justice Alito’s reliance on Brumfield does not undermine that conclusion because Brumfield supports habeas relief when an impermissible threshold rule prevents development of the constitutionally required, fuller inquiry, even if States retain discretion over ultimate factfinding.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly emphasize Hall’s holding that a State may not use an IQ-70 cutoff, ignoring SEM, to foreclose the adaptive-functioning inquiry; if the state court had plainly treated “70” as dispositive, I would view that as an unreasonable application. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, § 2254(d)(1) asks a narrower question under Richter/Lockyer: whether no fairminded jurist could read the state decision as an evidence-based assessment of multiple scores and the record rather than an impermissible bright-line rule. Brumfield, as Justice Jackson invokes it, shows some threshold denials can be unreasonable, yet it does not clearly establish a categorical habeas requirement to proceed to a full adaptive-functioning inquiry whenever any SEM-adjusted range touches 70. Given Atkins’s delegation to the States and the generality of Hall for AEDPA purposes on this record, I cannot say the state court crossed the “objectively unreasonable” line.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: Hall condemns a rigid IQ-70 gate that ignores SEM and thereby forecloses any adaptive-functioning inquiry in the borderline range. But under AEDPA, Chief Justice Roberts is right that the question is not whether the state court used the best clinical methodology, but whether its adjudication was an objectively unreasonable application of clearly established holdings at the time under Richter/Lockyer; Atkins expressly left implementation latitude to the States. Even crediting Justice Jackson’s invocation of Brumfield, that case illustrates when a threshold denial becomes unreasonable on an especially compelling record, not a clearly established rule that any SEM overlap automatically compels moving to prong two on habeas. On this record, fairminded jurists could disagree whether the state court applied an impermissible bright line versus a debatable evidentiary assessment across multiple scores and other evidence, which is enough to bar relief under § 2254(d)(1).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan most forcefully argue that the state court’s step-one analysis functioned as the IQ-70 “gate” Hall held unconstitutional, and that AEDPA cannot insulate that categorical cutoff. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes through Richter and Lockyer, § 2254(d)(1) asks whether the state court unreasonably applied clearly established holdings, not whether its screening approach was the best reading of Hall; Hall clearly forbids treating 70 as conclusive in the face of SEM, yet it does not clearly establish that any SEM-overlap or any score in the low-70s compels a full adaptive-functioning inquiry regardless of how the state court assessed multiple scores and the broader record. Justice Jackson’s invocation of Brumfield underscores that some threshold denials can be unreasonable, but it does not supply a square, outcome-determinative holding that converts Hall’s anti-bright-line principle into a mandatory procedure on habeas where fairminded jurists could disagree about whether the state court applied a prohibited cutoff or made a debatable evidentiary judgment. On this record, that space for fairminded disagreement is enough to keep me with Petitioner under AEDPA’s constraint.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’ strongest point—echoed by Justices Gorsuch and Kavanaugh—is that Richter/Lockyer require us to deny habeas if fairminded jurists could view the state court as doing record-based evaluation rather than enforcing a bright-line 70 cutoff. But that characterization is the problem: where the state court’s step-one analysis functionally treats “above 70” as dispositive without accounting for the SEM and thereby prevents reaching adaptive functioning for a score whose range includes 70, it is applying the very gate Hall held unconstitutional, not merely weighing competing evidence within Atkins’s implementation space. Justice Alito’s invocation of Brumfield does not move me the other way; Brumfield reinforces that an unreasonably rigid threshold screen that blocks the fuller Atkins inquiry can warrant relief even under AEDPA when the process creates an intolerable risk of executing an intellectually disabled person. Under my procedural-fairness, consequence-sensitive approach, AEDPA deference cannot be stretched to insulate a state adjudication that operationalizes a clinically discredited bright line into a categorical bar.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal habeas court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. Atkins recognized a categorical Eighth Amendment bar but left the detailed diagnostic implementation to the States, and neither Atkins nor this Court’s later decisions clearly established (for § 2254(d)(1) purposes) that IQ scores in the 70–75 range require proceeding to adaptive-functioning proof in every case. Given Richter’s requirement of strong deference to reasonable state-court adjudications and Lockyer’s warning against treating general principles as mandates for particular outcomes, I would not displace the state court’s determination on this record. A narrow ruling preserving institutional legitimacy would reverse on AEDPA grounds without deciding the best substantive rule for initial (non-habeas) Atkins litigation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal habeas court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, this Court’s clearly established law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter; Lockyer v. Andrade. Atkins held only that the Eighth Amendment forbids executing the intellectually disabled, but it left the relevant standards to the States and did not clearly establish any rule requiring that IQ scores in the 70–75 range automatically open the door to adaptive-functioning evidence on habeas. Given that Hall and Moore post-date many state adjudications and, in any event, do not clearly impose a rigid downward adjustment to the bottom of the SEM for every score, the Eleventh Circuit’s approach insufficiently respected AEDPA deference and improperly second-guessed the state court’s application of Atkins.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal habeas court may not grant relief unless the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court precedent. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter; Lockyer v. Andrade. Atkins left to the States the task of developing and enforcing standards for intellectual disability, and Hall/Brumfield—while rejecting a rigid, conclusive IQ cutoff that forecloses consideration of the SEM—did not clearly establish that IQ scores consistently in the 70–75 range compel a federal court, on habeas, to revisit the state court’s weighing of multiple scores and adaptive-functioning evidence. Given that Brumfield itself suggested a higher IQ score could make the state court’s determination reasonable, the Eleventh Circuit’s approach insufficiently respected AEDPA deference and improperly expanded Atkins beyond what § 2254(d)(1) permits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia forbids executing the intellectually disabled, and Hall v. Florida makes clear the Eighth Amendment does not permit a rigid IQ cutoff at 70; courts must account for the standard error of measurement and then consider the broader clinical picture, including adaptive functioning. Where valid IQ scores fall in the 70–75 range, Hall and Moore v. Texas require consideration of adaptive deficits rather than foreclosing the inquiry at step one. Under AEDPA, 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), a state decision that treats 70 as a strict bar (or otherwise refuses to consider adaptive-functioning evidence for scores within the SEM range) is an unreasonable application of clearly established Eighth Amendment law as articulated in Hall and reinforced in Moore. Given the grave, irreversible punishment and the heightened risk of wrongful execution for vulnerable defendants, a habeas court may consider adaptive-functioning and related evidence when IQ scores are near the cutoff.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Atkins v. Virginia bars execution of the intellectually disabled, and Hall v. Florida makes clear that States (and reviewing courts) may not treat an IQ score of 70 as a rigid cutoff; when valid scores fall within the test’s standard error of measurement above 70, the Eighth Amendment requires allowing consideration of additional evidence, including adaptive functioning. Given that principle, a state-court decision refusing to look beyond valid 70–75 scores to the broader clinical picture risks being an unreasonable application of clearly established law under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1), even while AEDPA demands substantial deference (Harrington v. Richter; Lockyer v. Andrade). The workable, textually coherent approach is to permit the adaptive-functioning inquiry in the borderline range rather than making IQ dispositive, while still leaving States discretion over the ultimate standards and factfinding so long as they do not impose an unconstitutional bright line. On this record, the Eleventh Circuit’s consideration of adaptive deficits alongside borderline IQ scores aligns with Hall’s requirement to account for measurement error and avoid excluding potentially intellectually disabled offenders from Atkins’ protection.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal court may grant relief only if the state court’s decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, “clearly established Federal law” as determined by this Court. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Williams v. Taylor; Harrington v. Richter. Atkins announced a substantive Eighth Amendment bar but expressly left to the States the task of developing procedures and evidentiary standards for identifying intellectual disability; and while Hall v. Florida rejected a rigid IQ-70 cutoff that forecloses consideration of the standard error of measurement and related evidence, it does not clearly establish that any petitioner with valid scores in the 70–75 range must be permitted to proceed to a full adaptive-functioning inquiry in a way that overrides a state court’s reasonable application of its own Atkins framework. Given the separation-of-powers limits AEDPA imposes on federal habeas courts and the requirement of substantial deference, the Eleventh Circuit’s approach appears to expand Atkins/Hall beyond what was clearly established at the relevant time and to second-guess a permissible state-court determination.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal habeas court may grant relief only if the state court decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter. Although Hall v. Florida and Moore instruct that States must account for the IQ test’s standard error of measurement and then consider adaptive-functioning evidence when scores fall within the relevant range, those decisions post-date many state-court adjudications and do not permit a federal court to override a reasonable state application of Atkins absent clearly established law at the time. Given AEDPA’s demanding deference and the Court’s instruction that relief is unavailable where fairminded jurists could disagree (Richter; Lockyer v. Andrade), the Eleventh Circuit’s approach risks substituting its own view of the clinical evidence for the state court’s, rather than identifying an objectively unreasonable application of controlling precedent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under AEDPA, a federal habeas court may grant relief only if the state court decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established Supreme Court law. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); Harrington v. Richter. Atkins recognized a constitutional bar on executing the intellectually disabled but left substantial implementation discretion to the States, and Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas (2017/2019) require consideration of the standard error of measurement and adaptive-functioning evidence only insofar as a State may not employ a rigid IQ cutoff that forecloses that evidence when the score’s range includes 70. Where the petitioner’s valid IQ scores are largely in the 70–75 range and the claim asks the federal court to expand Atkins/Hall/Moore beyond that clear holding or to reweigh the clinical evidence, AEDPA deference precludes relief absent a plainly unreasonable state-court application.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Hall v. Florida and Moore v. Texas, the Eighth Amendment forbids rigid IQ cutoffs and requires courts to account for the standard error of measurement; when a valid score in the 70–75 range has a lower bound at or below 70, the court must proceed to consider adaptive-functioning evidence rather than treating prong one as dispositive. That framework, grounded in Atkins v. Virginia’s incorporation of clinical standards, makes it procedurally unfair and substantively unreliable to bar full intellectual-disability proof solely because observed IQ scores are slightly above 70. On federal habeas, AEDPA (28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1)) demands deference, but a state-court rule that effectively precludes adaptive-deficits inquiry despite Hall/Moore’s command can be an unreasonable application of clearly established law. Given the practical consequence—risking execution of an intellectually disabled person—federal courts may consider adaptive-functioning and related evidence when IQ scores fall in the SEM-adjusted 70–75 range.
